hints: Focus on what happens to electrons when a metal forms a positive ion and a non-metal forms a negative ion.
Rubidium (atomic number 37) loses one electron to make $\text{Rb}^+$, while bromine (atomic number 35) gains one electron to make $\text{Br}^-$.
Think how losing a whole shell or adding extra repulsion changes size, then compare each atom to its own ion.
walkthrough:
**Identify the two ions**

Well done for spotting the clue about 36 electrons. That tells us exactly which ions form.

$$\text{Rb (37 e}^-\text{) } \rightarrow \text{Rb}^+ \text{ (36 e}^-\text{) + e}^-$$
$$\text{Br (35 e}^-\text{) + e}^- \rightarrow \text{Br}^- \text{ (36 e}^-\text{)}$$

**Compare rubidium atom and ion**

When Rb loses its outer 5s electron, it loses a whole shell and has fewer electrons for the same nuclear charge to pull in. So the cation is pulled in tighter.

$$\text{radius of Rb atom > radius of Rb}^+$$

**Compare bromine atom and ion**

When Br gains an electron, the nuclear charge stays the same but there is more electron-electron repulsion in the same shell. So the electron cloud expands.

$$\text{radius of Br atom < radius of Br}^-$$

**Pick the matching row**

Putting it together: rubidium atomic > ionic, and bromine atomic < ionic. That is the only row that fits both trends.

options.A: Incorrect. The bromine part is right ($\text{Br}^-$ is larger than Br), but rubidium is wrong. $\text{Rb}^+$ has lost its outer shell, so it must be smaller than the Rb atom, not larger.
options.B: Incorrect. Both parts are reversed. A positive ion is never larger than its parent atom, and a negative ion is never smaller than its parent atom.
options.C: Correct. $\text{Rb}^+$ is smaller than Rb because loss of the 5s electron removes a shell and increases effective pull. $\text{Br}^-$ is larger than Br because the extra electron increases repulsion with no extra protons. So atomic > ionic for rubidium and atomic < ionic for bromine.
options.D: Incorrect. The rubidium part is right ($\text{Rb}^+$ is smaller than Rb), but bromine is wrong. $\text{Br}^-$ gains an electron with the same 35 protons, so repulsion expands it and it must be larger than the Br atom.
